header.title: ORATIO PRO CURREPTIUNE VITÆ. FLENDA SEMPER PECCATA (Appendix XVIII): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Incertus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp1442.tmp1442.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1442.tmp1442.opp-lat: §4: 'rigans' has the editor's suggestion 'rigo' (I water); the sense is the same. 'praeceptus' is unclear (perhaps praereptus or pressus); rendered 'seized by'. The 'alphabet' refers to an alphabetic prayer preceding this text. §8: 'in hac reddit justiorem' is awkward; read as 'renders him more just'. §10: 'Haec secundum similitudinem foliis est' appears corrupt; the comparison intended (perhaps 'a second plank after shipwreck', a common image for penitence) cannot be recovered with confidence, so the gap is marked [...]. Numerous OCR errors (e.g. desulo subdistrictionis = desudo, sub districtionis; dilu v. = diluit) have been silently corrected.

Line 12: 'curati Deo' read as 'coram Deo'. Line 13 is numbered '15' in the scan, evidently for 13. 'renovata morum pravitate' ('the depravity being renewed') makes poor sense; translated as 'remota' (put away). 'minor inventa mortificetur' is obscure; rendered literally. Line 14: 'nec regimine utor, nec consilium' appears defective (a verb such as 'invenio' may be missing); 'anteritatem' read as 'austeritatem', 'ne notis' as 'ne nolis', 'incitas' as 'incitat'. Line 18: 'Domine Ini Jesu' read as 'Domine mi Jesu' (or 'Deus'); 'essecrando mortem non leUDis' is corrupt, read as 'execrando mortem non laetaris'; the purpose clause 'ut homo inveniretur, qui utique perierat' is rendered as the sense seems to require.

Line 19 opens with a stray 'tU.', apparently a fragment or footnote mark, left untranslated. Scanning errors read as: 'diteor' = diffiteor, 'contido' = confido, 'moliar' = moriar, 'compræstabilis' = præstabilis. Line 21: 'retinere dicis' and 'ætate' in the clause introducing Jer. 2:23 seem corrupt; rendered by sense. The Jeremiah and Isaiah quotations follow the text as given, which departs from the Vulgate in places (e.g. 'thronum gloriæ' for 'thronum gratiae' in Heb. 4).

Several scanning errors read as evident (e.g. 'principatior' as 'chief', 'sica' as 'sic a', 'multa' in §34 read as a verb of cleansing, 'resera' in §34 taken as 'reseca', cut away). §31-32 describe the speaker as imprisoned in chains; §32 is corrupt in places: 'mortali aeternum dedit carcerem ferrumque perenne' and 'quia non dictum: Revertamur impertire veniam perituro' are rendered tentatively, and 'contra impietatem, qua licet juste morior' is obscure. In §33 'ut hic corda principum corpori placetur inflectere' appears corrupt; rendered by sense. 'Non affliges in aeternum proximum tuum' is not an identifiable biblical text.

Many scanning errors corrected silently. 35: 'sentina, rorem' read as 'seminatorem' (sower); 'repede' as 'repelle'. 37: 'loris ei me procedat' read as 'foris a me non procedat'; 'soptatur' as 'sopiatur', 'tespoatur' as 'respuatur'. 38: 'ne me perspectem boni fallat' read as 'ne me sub specie boni fallat'; 'amico subinde rni silentio' as 'amico subinde uti silentio'. 41: 'iturum pravitate comptissimum extrema vim' is corrupt; translated tentatively (with the edition's 'vita'); 'flagratores' read as 'flagella'; 'junia' as 'jam'. 39: 'nullius explorare rectam semitam' is odd as printed; translated literally.

Scanning errors read as: 'deine libi' = deinde tibi; 'compulisti'; 'conliterer' = confiterer; 'nunu' = nunc; 'lucris' = quaeris; 'retrigerii' = refrigerii. 'netum' is read as fletum ('weeping'); gemitum is also possible. The sense of 'actio' versus 'acceptio' (performing penance versus its formal acceptance) is unclear. 'semitam lucis nemorosam' ('shady path of light') is odd; luminosam may be meant. 'eri u-lum' is garbled; it is taken as a word for 'wanderer' (e.g. erraticum or erronem).

nodes.text: APPENDIX XVIII.
PRAYER FOR THE CORRECTION OF LIFE. SINS MUST ALWAYS BE WEPT FOR.

1. God, author of all wonders, Father of mercies and of consolation, refreshment in tribulation, forestalled by whose grace a man considers his sins, laments them, and amends them; by whose regard and gift he begins to do good, to avoid and reject evil, to follow justice and turn aside from iniquity, to desire things everlasting and shudder at things that will perish, to confess your mercies and renounce his own impieties; for man has nothing of his own, but his conversion and progress are your gift; nor can anyone be corrected by himself, but by you; as the prophet says: I know, Lord, that a man's way is not his own, nor is it a man's to walk and direct his steps (Jer. 10:23); and the Apostle says: It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. 9:16); and you yourself say: I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be merciful to whom it pleases me (Exod. 33:19).

2. Be present, then, to my supplications; attend to my entreaty. And what I ask, accomplish graciously, and attend [to it] appeased. For you drew me out of the snares of the world, and led me out of the net of sins. You opened my mouth to confess to you, when I was bound by all sins; and you made me understand how, or for what, I should beseech you. You put confidence in my heart to ask for what my soul needs, since (as the prophet said): Willing mercy, you turn back and have mercy, forgetting the evils of men and passing over sins in kindness (Mic. 7:18-19); and you yourself said: Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you (Matt. 7:7).

3. For he who grants leave to be asked and knocked upon is without doubt ready to give and to open; nor is he grudging in bestowing who cries out to those who have not that they should ask; and for this reason he will afterwards repent of his want who now neglects to obtain from the steward the fitting remedies to be given to him. Therefore I cannot keep silent, admonished by the touch of grace coming upon me. For I confess, Lord, that your mercy forestalled me, unworthy as I was, and while I lay on the bed of the many sins of this world, weighed down by a kind of deadly sleep, you sent your grace with the crack of scourges to rouse me, torpid with damnable sloth, so that, awakened with open eyes, recognising in myself no sustenance of good work, I might come to you to seek the nourishment of life, lest want coming upon me should choke me at the last.

4. Therefore, rising up to you with cries of lamentation, I knock with manifold prayer at the ears of your pity, through the alphabet which I set out before, watering each of its letters with a river of tears. For dread of your judgement has driven me to weep long, and your grace has made me pray with confidence, believing that in you, my God, I shall pass over the wall of all my iniquities which have surrounded me, and, seized by the afflictions of my straits, shall pass through to the breadth of the widest joy, namely not of this world but of the world to come. For this reason I will not cease to entreat you until you have mercy on me and save my soul, which confesses to you today, set in the valley of weeping, that you have brought me in; for not by my merit but by your gift I have come to the cloister of the strictest penitence, and have entered its fountain of tears to wash away the various stains of wickedness; [penitence] which was bestowed on me not at my asking but by your granting, and which, through your mercy's provision, I found when I was not yet seeking it.

5. Behold, now for no small time I sweat in the heat of its affliction; I labour under the rule of its strictness. While I am tried by it with daily examination, its pressure draws great groans from me, and it compels me more and more to weep because I have sinned, and teaches me to give you thanks continually for your great patience, with which you long bore with me in my wantonness, and kept a time of correction in which I might abandon transgression and be converted, lest, pursuing sin unceasingly, I should perish with sin for ever; and now, teaching me mercifully with your rod, you work my salvation, withdrawing my life from corruption and my soul from destruction, that I might know that the choice of good things is to pass by wicked ones.

6. And trusting in this I hope that, as you brought on the tribulations of penitence, so you will also impart the mercies of pardon. And not only that, but I also bless your holy name, because you put off the event of death, lest in the torpor of sin I should sink into eternal punishment; and you came to my aid, providing from afar the remedy of my cure, in that you handed over my soul, torn by a pestilent ulcer, to be healed by the medicines of this penitence. For good to me is its goading, which teaches me to flee past offences and warns me to beware of future ones. Light I reckon the yoke of its burden, because it removes heavier torments than it inflicts, and while it presses in time, it redeems for eternity.

7. Lovable to me are its bonds, which now bind in a little, so as to make [me] free for ever. Pleasing are its outward squalors, because by their roughness the soul is cleansed within from its offences. And sweeter to me now is its bitterness than the sweetness of a luxurious life was in the past, because through that life the soul is choked, but through this one there is rising again from such a death. What that defiled, this washes away. What that made bloody, this treats and heals. For if I saw a harmful wound outwardly in my body, or felt some pain of the bowels within, I would run at once to the physician, I would hand over my flesh to be cut with pains by the knife and burned with the red-hot cautery, and for the sake of restoring health I would not refuse to drink the bitterest antidotes.

8. Why then should I bear these things with vexation, through which the soul is restored from eternal destruction to everlasting salvation? What shall I render to you, most loving God, lover of men and merciful justifier of sinners, for the things you have bestowed on me? I will take the cup of salvation, and therefore call upon your name with praises; since you have led my steps back into the way of life, I will not cease to give you thanks. For this is the way by which one runs back from the underworld to heaven, returns from sin to justice, is recalled from offence to your grace; and, to conclude briefly, this is the repair of every ruin. This, finally, when the publican prayed in the temple, surpassed the righteous deeds of the Pharisee, and rendered him more just; this led Lazarus through temporal scourges to eternal rest.

9. To you, Lord, be praise and glory, who strike and heal, wound and cure. You give passing pain, and after a little while refresh with eternal joy, since you are just and loving: just, because you never spare the one who sins; loving, because you do not withhold mercy from the penitent; again, you are just and loving, because first you amend a man from his sins here, and afterwards free him from eternal punishment. For, as I said before, you do not spare the sinner, since you either strike him with a temporal scourge for his cleansing, or leave him to be punished by eternal judgement, or the man himself, by repenting, punishes in himself what he wrongly committed; and so it is that you are said never to spare the one who sins. For no sin can be left unpunished, since sins deserve punishment; but either a man punishes it, and you free him; or, if he puts it off, you punish it, according to what the Apostle says: If we judged ourselves, we would surely not be judged. As if he said: If we separated ourselves from sin in this world, the future punishment of sin would not strike us.

10. It is necessary, then, for a man to punish sin, so as not to incur eternal punishment; for penitence (paenitentia) took its name from punishment (punitio), as if 'punitence', since the man himself by repenting punishes what he wrongly committed. For those who truly repent do nothing else than refuse to let what they did wrongly go unpunished. In this way indeed you spare those who do not spare themselves, you whose lofty and just judgement no despiser escapes. Now the perfection of penitence is to blot out the past and not to admit the future. This is, by a likeness, [...], so that if perhaps, through the devil's assault, some sin has crept in, it may be cleansed by its satisfaction. Satisfaction, moreover, is to shut out the causes and suggestions of sins, and not to repeat sin again. Penitence itself is to be done according to the nature of the offences; for as light sins are blotted out by secret prayer, so grave ones are remitted before the Church through penitence and satisfaction.

11. Hence, since the satisfaction of penitence is weighed by your judgement, not by human judgement, and the mercy of your pardon is hidden, it is necessary to weep without ceasing. Nor should the penitent ever have security about sin, because that is its enemy; for it gives birth to negligence, and negligence often leads the unwary back to past vices; but he ought to be as ready to repent as he was prone to sin, and to advance as much higher through humility as he is known to have fallen lower through pride; and to lament not only that he did the evil he ought not, but also that he did not do the good he ought. For this thing justifies the most careful worker, not the idle one; for true penitence is anxious with greater care in every holy work.

12. [True penitence] has no laughter at all; it does not admit idle tales, nor is it stained by desires and wanton deeds; it does not covet earthly things, it longs for heavenly ones, it thinks on its end, it is always intent on the judgement to come, and how it may appear worthily before God, this it attends to daily; it serves as a soldier for God alone, it is entangled in no business of the world. It is most constant in vigils and prayers, practised in fasting, moderate in food and drink, diligent in labour and reading, unfailing in charity, perpetual in chastity, most truthful in speech, restrained in swearing; it is kind and patient, it is not kindled by envy, it is not overcome by anger, it shuns boasting, loves humility, does not repay insult, hates avarice, flees vainglory, detests pride, spurns joys, and embraces groans, sighs and tribulations, knowing that your mercy is not granted to the negligent or to those who laugh, but is given to the afflicted and contrite of heart, as you yourself say: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt. 5:5). And again: Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep (James 4:9-10). And the Apostle says: Be wretched, and mourn, and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.

13. It is certain indeed that every fault is dissolved by weeping, if, with the depravity of conduct put away, past wickedness is not repeated. For it is not enough to depart from evil, unless doing good also follows; as it is written: Turn aside from evil, and do good (Ps. 36:27). And elsewhere: Cease to act perversely, learn to do well (Isa. 1:16); so that, with the satisfaction of repentance set against sin, and at the same time the past wickedness covered and wrapped over by the goodness that follows, it may perish, and, found to be the lesser, may be put to death. Therefore, since through the satisfaction of weeping the fallen soul is raised up again, and by a washing of this kind recovers the dignity of its former brightness, it is fitting for me to increase my weeping, and to make my tears frequent over my often repeated iniquities, which I have committed countless times. For I do not think it enough for me to have wept in proportion to the abundance of my offences; for this reason I will lament my offences constantly in bitterness, if perhaps it may please you to cleanse me from them altogether. Would that the waters of my head were turned to blood, and that I might pour out blood instead of tears, so that I might wipe away cruel sins with cruel lamentations, sins by which I once wickedly wounded myself in sluggish folly.

14. Therefore my soul, anxious, is overthrown by immense weariness, and it has even withered, terrified by fear of your fury. My life is turned into the juice of wormwood, my innards overflow with gall and vinegar, my heart is corrupted by deep pains, sigh is taken up by sigh, and groan rushes upon groan. Through fear of punishments to come, and the present misery of scourges, I am bowed down and humbled to the end; nor can I lift my head, weighed down by a manifold burden. Death stands, and my immense crimes stand before my eyes; and there is nothing from which redemption could come. Ineffably troubled because of this, I have no guidance, nor counsel; the distress of oppression brings [me] to the very point of despair, and, like one standing on a spider's thread, the state of my mind sways as if to collapse, at times fearing, because of the severity of my faults, that you will not pardon, at times trusting, because of the gentleness of your mercies, that you will resolve to free [me]; and between hope and fear there is no small agitation of my heart, for if you wish to destroy, justice urges you, but if you wish to save, mercy invites you; and although present scourges absolve one who has turned from sins, yet my mind wavers for this reason, lest my wounds be not enough to purge away all my offences; and the subtlety of your great wisdom inflicts punishments outwardly just as it sees faults inwardly.

15. But who can be at rest about your judgement, when before the strictness of your examination not even the justice of the just is secure? If an account must be given even for an idle word, how shall I be secure, who have committed capital evils? There is no security at all in my mind before the face of your judgement, nor peace in my conscience before the face of my sins. Therefore my contrition is great as the sea, because my wound is most grievous. I seek a harbour of escape, and I find no way to get back out of the snare of Satan's deceit; he has entangled my feet, and I can in no way prevail. I cry out, overcome by a multitude of pains, and there is none to rescue. I toil in mourning and groaning, fettered, and abandoned in the distress of prison, and there is none to console. Alas for me! Alas, wretched and unhappy one! whom most just punishments terrify, whom deserved vengeances crush, whom scourges and rebukes rightly batter, whom various afflictions of miseries fittingly lay waste, because I have sinned wickedly, offended cruelly, strayed violently, fallen heavily! Woe to me, who have polluted myself with such evils, defiled myself with so great a wickedness! who did not have the wisdom to avoid drinking the poison of the devil's cup, which has killed the soul!

16. And now I would not need to be brought to life again, if I had guarded most circumspectly against being pierced by his lances, and I would now be without a wound, and would not be seeking medicine, if I had understood how to flee and not be caught in his snares; then I would now be free, and would not be crying out for release. Unhappy man that I am, who will free me from such great bonds, and from the peril of this death, except your grace, almighty Father, through Jesus Christ our Lord, whom you appointed as redemption for the salvation of the world; in whose justice and sanctification all iniquity is blotted out, and the dominion of death is made void? who has become (as the prophet says) a rock, a refuge for hedgehogs (Ps. 103:18), that is, the support and salvation of the sinner; of whom John also says: If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just, and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world (1 John 2:1); in whom all salvation has been established by you, as Peter says to the Jews: There is salvation in no other; nor is there any other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved. He holds the keys of death and of hell, he unbars the gates of the abyss and shuts the doors of darkness; he opens, and no one shuts, he shuts, and no one opens; to him you have given all power in heaven and on earth. At his name every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth; he is the man of your will, in whose hand everything that is pleasing before you is accomplished. He, being the radiance of glory and the image of your substance, bearing all things by the word of his power, sits at your right hand, making purification for sins and interceding with you for sinners; he is the beginning and end of the whole of things (Acts 4:12; Rev. 1:18; 3:7; Phil. 2:10; Heb. 1:3).

17. For before him no creature existed, and through him the whole creation was made and began to be, and he will be the consummation of all creation, when he brings an end to the world, and judgement; since he is the man whom you prepared to judge the living and the dead, and you judge no one, but have given all judgement to him; he alone has the power to destroy and to set free, because you were well pleased in him; you exalted him above all the heavens, and above every principality and power and dominion, giving him glory and honour, setting him over all the works of your hands, and subjecting all things under his feet; through whom all things were made and founded in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, by whom all things are held together, in whom they consist; through whom you founded the earth, established the heavens, closed the abyss, walled in the sea; for he is your wisdom and counsel, your power, your hand and your right hand, with the Holy Spirit creating together and giving life together, working together and giving life together to all things and to what is in all things, who proceeds ineffably from you and from the same Son of yours; in whom I too have faithfully believed from my earliest years; against whom I confess that I have sinned, and from whom I beg pardon in deep humility of heart.

18. Hence, Lord Jesus, since many are the mercies in your hand, and you do not allow anyone to perish, but will all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; since, abhorring death, you take no pleasure in the destruction of the living; and you do not will the ruin of man, but his salvation, and for this reason, humbling yourself, though you were God, you deigned to become man, so that man, who had surely perished, might be found. I have fittingly resolved that I must return to you from my transgressions; receive me into your hands as I return with weeping before you; graciously accept the prayers of my confessions, and save one who confesses; do not despise [my] penitence, Lord; I repent of having strayed, and I grieve now that I long ago foolishly committed most wicked things; but do not turn your face away from me, for, if you will, you can cleanse me; for yours is the power of putting to death and giving life, of freeing, of binding and loosing; I have handed over my soul to be bound by the bonds of various crimes, and, as you see, I have wounded it with most wicked sin; loose, Lord, loose now the chains on my neck, bound by which in many ways I have long cried to you, and in pity apply medicine to the laid-open wound.

Restore to me my former health, and let my soul live by your remedy. You indeed declare my wound grievous, and I do not deny that it is grievous; yet I trust without doubt that you can heal it, for I believe that nothing is difficult for you, nothing impossible, since I have learned, on your own testimony, that all things are possible with the Lord, when you declare that it is easy for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. I have sinned, Lord, I have sinned greatly, and for this reason, as you yourself foresee, my tribulations have been enlarged, tormenting my heart night and day. For the heap of my guilt, or of my sins, is not small; hence my many groans, and my mind most sorrowful from the overthrow of great disturbance; but through consideration of your great and innumerable mercies your kindness has directed me, as I struggle little by little to rise from the stain of peril, to the hope of pardon, so that, hesitating in nothing in faith, I may ask forgiveness, and may not die, but live.

20. Therefore, having returned to the one who struck me and who has power over my wounds, that is, to you, my Lord also, I bend my knees to you, and with earnest prayer, with confession of penitence, in the contrition of fasting, I beseech you, giving glory to your name in most frequent praise and blessing. For this you taught me in the solitude of my enclosure. Will you not in this way repair the fall of my ruin? I fully believe that you will. I have hope, therefore, in confession, in which, most steadfastly made firm, I have not despaired, nor shall I despair, but I enjoy perfect trust; by which, wickedness being scraped out and abolished from the heart, I may, my petition having first been made, come back to life through you from every death of crimes, and, confession being made, be purified from all the filth of sins, because you are faithful in your words, and what has proceeded from your lips you will not make void; for your mercies are not exhausted, nor is the confidence of rising cut off in this life for those who fall by whatever mischance; for in every kind of sin you have set a return, and have kept penitence as the remedy of the sinner, saying: I do not will the death of the wicked man, but that he turn back and live (Ezek. 33:11). And again: If, when I say to the wicked man, You shall die, he turns from his wickedness and does penance, does justice, walks in the commandments of life, and so on, he shall surely live, and shall not die (ibid., 14).

21. And in Jeremiah: Suddenly I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to root it up and destroy and scatter it; if that nation does penance for its evil, which I have spoken against it, I too shall repent of the evil that I planned to do to it (Jer. 18:7); and the rest. And again: Behold, I am fashioning evil against you, and devising a design against you; let each one turn back from his evil way, and direct your ways and your pursuits. They said, By no means, we have despaired; we shall go after our own thoughts, and each of us will do the depravity of his evil heart. And to Jerusalem, when the people, prone to every most wicked crime, were turning aside after idols, you say (Jer. 2:23): See your ways in the valley, know what you have done; a swift runner tracing out your ways; a wild ass used to the wilderness, in her soul's [desire], snuffed up the wind of her love; no one will turn her away (see Isidoriana, loc. cit., n. 31).

22. It is commonly said: If a man dismisses his wife, and she, departing from him, takes another husband, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have played the harlot with many lovers; yet return to me, says the Lord. Lift up your eyes straight ahead, and see where you have prostituted yourself; you sat waiting for them like a robber in the wilderness, you have polluted the land with your fornications and with your wickedness; therefore the drops of the rains were withheld, and there was no late rain; you have got a harlot's brow, you refused to blush. Therefore at least from now on call to me: You are my father, and the guide of my virginity. Will you be angry for ever, or will you persist to the end?

23. And again: Return, rebellious Israel, says the Lord, to me, and I shall not turn my face away from you, for I am holy, says the Lord, and I shall not be angry for ever. Turn, you who return, for I am your husband; I shall take you to myself; if you take away your stumbling-blocks from before my face, you shall not be moved (Jer. 3:12). And you yourself, through Jeremiah, to the people persisting in sin and unwilling to return, still holding back your patience, say: Do not withhold a word, if perhaps they may hear, and each may turn back from his evil way, and I may repent of what I planned to do to them because of the wickedness of their pursuits. And in Isaiah he says: I am the one who speaks justice, and I am a champion to save. If you return and are at rest, you will be saved. And again: Return to me, do not forget me, and I will redeem you. I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I shall not remember your sins; for I know that you will surely transgress, and I called you a transgressor from the womb; for my name's sake I shall put my fury far off, and with my praise I shall bridle you, so that you do not perish.

24. And again to sinners, that they may be washed clean through penitence, he says: Wash yourselves, be clean, take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely, learn to do well; and the rest; and if your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow, and if they are red as crimson, they shall be clean as wool. And to the transgressing and offending people, unwilling to be converted, of whom you had already said that for the enormity of their crimes your wrath would destroy them, you say in Hosea: My heart is turned within me, my repentance is likewise stirred within me; I shall not act in the fury of my wrath. I shall not turn to destroy you, for I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst (Hos. 11:8). For if to a people turned away and unrepentant, who, abandoning you, had subjected themselves to all abominations and impurities and idols, you, bearing with them in such patience, offered such mercy, how much more placable can you be towards one who has not turned away from you, and, repentant for his sin, bowed down, beseeches you?

25. Rightly, therefore, another prophet cries: Turn to the Lord, for he is kind and merciful, patient and of great mercy, and ready to relent over evil (Joel 2:13). And David says: The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and very merciful; he has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor will he repay us according to our iniquities (Ps. 102:8). And in Solomon: The Lord has had mercy on the penitent (Ecclus. 12:3). And again: For the Lord is kind and merciful, and forgives sins in the time of tribulation to all who seek him in truth (Ecclus. 2:15). Hence also the Apostle, with the testimony of the prophet, exhorts, saying: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts; for we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathise with our weaknesses; let us therefore approach with confidence to the throne of his glory, that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help (Heb. 4:7). And you, Lord, cry to those labouring in iniquity and burdened with the weight of sins: Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). And many other things of this kind, which it would take long to write out from all the Scriptures.

26. The Lord, then, of such patience and such great mercies I shall seek with longing, approach boldly, follow gladly, embrace strongly, hold humbly, by no means let go, beseech confidently; in whose compassion and mercy there lies open to me, by the way of penitence, a return from death to life, a running back from hell to heaven, an entrance from darkness to light. This, therefore, Lord, I ask first of all, and so I shall pass on to the rest: give me a most devoted resolve of mind for repenting, which may be acceptable and pleasing before you; give the compunction of humility, so that my mind may sigh from love of you, and, the hardness of the heart dissolved, may groan over its wound. Rouse all the senses of my inmost heart, that they may cry to you with the strength of an inner voice, if perhaps at some time you may hear one who beseeches; let the sighs of my breast be stirred, and let a murmuring groan sound in your ears. Loosen the reins of my eyes, and let my eyelids, flowing with the ample stream of a fountain, pour forth waters, so that the guilt of all my crimes may be washed away by the onrush of tears, and let the channels of the veins of my head run without failing, until all the uncleanness of iniquity is wiped away.

27. Let my mouth be filled with the words of a most truthful confession, so that, delighted by them, you may be eager to spare in clemency and not delay to grant pardon; and let my repentance become fruitful for me, bringing joy to birth out of mourning, bringing pardon out of want, and leading rest out of labour, so that by the narrow path of prison afflictions you may lead me to the entrance of life, and may let me receive, in the bond of an iron chain, the release of my sins. Behold, Lord, the time of confession is at hand, and the days of remission are here, in which the promised pardon is granted to those who ask; for what more shall I confess to you, since I do not deny that I am more wicked than all the wicked, whom you will judge to be just by comparison with me? For there has lacked the vice of no crime among sins, of no misdeed, with whose filth I have not defiled myself, by whose contagion I have not been polluted: headlong into lust, shameless in wantonness, frequent in luxury, unblushing in fornication, daily piling crime on crime, I have not ceased to add worse things to the worst, cruel in will, depraved in mind, dishonourable in conduct, polluted in heart, and blasphemous in lips, wrathful and insolent.

28. Because of this I am confounded, and I blush now to raise my eyes, judging myself unworthy to look upon the heavenly stars. But act for the glory of your name, my God. Grant me, as I confess to you, pardon for salvation, and grant the remedy of indulgence, so that, made propitious and placable, you may blot out all the misdeeds of my sins, and not seek out my iniquities, which the slippery age of my youth and ignorance committed, raw, lascivious, vain and foolish, prone to evil, most sluggish towards good, swift towards death, slow towards life, to which the works of light are hateful and those of darkness most beloved, which loves to fall and neglects to rise; salvation is bitter to it, and perdition sweet. Release, Lord, the guilty one bound by inextricable knots, and, the snares of crimes broken, make him go away free, so that you may save me in your good will, and I may not perish in my malice, nor go down into hell, from which there is no further ascent; for your mercy is more copious than the abundance of my sins. And you are more exceedingly kind than I am wicked. I indeed am malicious and headlong, but you are gentle and patient; I am prone and frail for falling, you are ready and strong for raising up. If you look back on what has been done, you would at once judge [me] to perish; if you attend to my present will and vow, I believe that you will judge to save me, because you have directed my heart in your desires, which you see my mind serving more ardently, for my soul thirsts for you, and my flesh likewise delights [in you].

29. Redeem me, Lord my God, from all my distresses, and may it please you to snatch me from destruction. Call me back from the gate of death, and lead me back in the eternal way, that I may run in the path of your commandments and walk in your truth. Let not the cavern of darkness hold me back, nor the pit or caves of the abyss shut me in; but open to me, light of light, the entrance of eternal life. Unbar the gate, for you are God, receiving the tears of a contrite heart and accepting the humiliation of the penitent. For you will not be called kind among those who do not sin, but when you have turned to the impious and had mercy on the sinner [to free him] from evil. I have always fallen into worse, and flowed down from bad things to worse; but you are a very skilled craftsman, knowing how to fashion for yourself a useful vessel out of a useless one; for this is your work from the beginning, to make the just out of the wicked and to form the worthy out of the unworthy; to raise again the crushed, and to repair the ancient ruins of those who slip; for, as you yourself declare, The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill (Matt. 9:12); this cause also made you descend into this world, to save sinners, of whom I am the chief; and if then, with the pains of your passion, you willed to save enemies, adversaries, the estranged and the impious, could you now destroy friends who have turned back and repent? Far from it. Truly it delights you to pardon sinners, if they turn back, you who did not refuse to undergo death for sinners. For you would by no means have mounted the cross for the wicked, if you refused to spare the wicked.

30. For if you did not refuse to the unrepentant and tearless legion of demons the herd of swine it asked for, how much more readily will you be prompt to grant pardon of sins to a faithful soul imploring you with weeping? Trusting in this, I offer you the prayers and tears of my penitence: you will save me just as [you save] the others who repent of having failed. Or will the trust and promise of your kindness and pardon, through which all the converted families of the earth are saved, remain unfruitful in my case, or become dry and void in me alone? Will your great clemency, which can never be lessened by giving, nor is constrained by the effect of any want, become insufficient in one penitent? Will you hold yourself back in me alone, so as not to bestow what is asked, made barren of the fruit of mercy? Will you be grieved against me for ever, for a sin of a short time, which, by the disposing of your providence, I repent of, cursing and abhorring it, since I am a creature from earth and ashes, corruptible and mortal, but you are God the creator, incorruptible and immortal? Will you, hardened in mercilessness, not hear one contrite and humbled, or will you judge it right to punish one who confesses to you, or decide to destroy one who entreats you? I shall not believe so, nor suspect that you wish it, for this is impious and against the nature of divine kindness. Therefore, suppliant and confident, I implore your mercy, that you may fulfil my petitions with kindly will.

31. Incline, Lord, your ear, and hear; open your eyes, and see my desolation. See the many afflictions and miseries which grind me as a cart grinds straw, devour [me] as moths devour wool, consume [me] as [fire consumes] rotten wood; and, softening your fury, hold back the scourge. Now have mercy on me, be appeased, and return; spare my soul, spare my sins. Do not forget me to the end, do not be angry with me for ever, do not forsake me utterly, nor abandon me in any way to perish, but restore your grace to me, and save me in the place of danger where my flesh lies, bound tight with iron, struck with blows, worn out by punishments, exhausted by sicknesses, deserted by human care, separated from companions, shut in by squared stones, given over by just judgement to a dunghill and stenches, exposed in darkness and deadly shadows to long-lasting miseries. All of which you yourself behold, who sit above the cherubim and gaze upon the abysses.

32. Already my crushing and my striking have become old and of long standing, and there is no one who remembers your kindness, nor anyone who, pricked in heart, reflects, saying: Now for the Lord's sake I will have pity on a mortal; [he has] given a mortal an eternal prison and perpetual iron. No mercy of rescue is reserved for me; I am condemned by an irrevocable judgement, for it has not been said: Let us turn back to grant pardon to one about to perish. Remember, Lord, your mercies towards me, and change this heavy and very harsh sentence, for you have said: You shall not afflict your neighbour for ever; for I desire mercy and not sacrifice; and against the impiety for which, though I justly die, you nevertheless, because you are kind, mercifully prepare the support of life; bestow, Lord, propitiously, divine help where human help has withdrawn; I alone am left to you; help me, solitary as I am. Do not be a stranger to me in the days of distress, nor abandon me in the time of tribulation; do not cease to guard me with protection, nor stop nourishing me with care.

33. Fix your eyes upon me, lest I perish; protect and quicken me; be for my soul and body alike the giver of life and life itself, and the healer and health of all my infirmities, so that I may live by the gift of your kindness, and praise you in my life before my brothers, until, appeased by your inspiration, the indignation of the one who afflicts me also rests; for you have power both here to bend the hearts of princes so that [they] may be appeased towards the body, and there to free the soul from future punishments, you to whom no one will say: What have you done? nor will anyone resist your judgement, nor withstand your will; nor indeed will anyone dare then to accuse the guilty one whom you now have absolved from his faults; but he will be blessed without any contradiction, as it is written: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin (Ps. 31:1-2); and the Apostle: If God, he says, is for us, who is against us? It is God who justifies; who is it who condemns (Rom. 8:33)? Test me, Lord, test me in the furnace of humiliation, in which you are examining one unworthy for a long while.

34. I ask only that you do not reject [me]; burn up the harmful rust of sins; scorch away the pernicious filth of crimes, so that from the adulterate mixture of lead you may draw out the purest, glowing gold; and hasten to rescue me thus by a temporal scourge; cut away the excesses of my faults, so that you leave nothing in the future to punish, but something to make blessed. Here, Lord God, [cleanse] me from all crimes, here wipe me clean from every filth of vices, here release me from every bond of sins, so that either, if you release me alive, I may depart purified, or, if you decide to call me, I may be taken up wholly cleansed. Rule my soul while it is placed in the body; receive it as it goes out from the body, and grant it to cleave to you for ever, so that a thing commended with many tears to you, its Lord God and creator, may in no way perish. But if a longer life is still kept for me in the flesh, let it be ordered with a new honour worthy of praise. Strip me of the foulness of all vices, and clothe [me] with the dignity of all virtues, casting in and planting the seeds of charity and kindness, of humility and continence. But of greed and avarice, vanity and arrogance, anger and impatience, and the other wickednesses, cut off the rotten old growths; prune away the superfluous, cut out the shameful, press down the proud, cut back the harmful and unfruitful, so that the bitterness of the evil tree, changed, may produce good sap; that after the harshness of troubles you may bring forth sweet fruits for yourself, so that what nature did not have before, it may henceforth offer as conferred by grace.

35. Put to flight from me the occasion of sinning, and stir up my care for the practice of good. Take away, again, the desire to sin, and shut out all carnal affections. Let there be in my soul no lust for foul pleasure, but let the love of most beautiful chastity dwell [there]. Let the ambition of this world be far from me, so that I may not turn aside from my resolve because of its hindrance. I desire that the grace of fear and love of you alone may always be in me, by whose fruit I may come to life again from all the deadliness of vices. For through fear one withdraws from evil, and through charity a good work is accomplished. And again, what charity works through love, fear guards, so that it may not perish through pride. Likewise charity hastens and joins [one] to God, and fear does not allow [one] to be separated from him. This is the holy fear that endures for ever and ever. Let harmful prosperity and the friendships of this world not come near me; but temper adversities, so that I may be able to bear them, since prosperity casts down, adversity instructs. Prosperity often entices the mind to sin, but adversity both holds [it] back from sin and always calls and urges [it] to hate the present life and to desire the future one. Therefore do not allow me any longer to be entangled in any business of the world, but, where I serve as a soldier for you alone, may I always serve you; may I worship you unceasingly, and sing psalms to you day and night. Drive back from me the sower of evil thoughts and the instigator of useless desires that are contrary to good intention, and against all his temptations and cunning deceptions set the defence of your help and protection, so that the devil, seeing me unbending in good perseverance, may withdraw confounded.

36. Allow me only to weep for all my sins, not to desire them. Make me hate what you hate, and embrace what you love. Let my mind obey your commandments, and let my will agree with your will, so that nothing shameful, nothing unjust, nothing dishonourable, nothing unseemly or impious, arising in the delight of my conscience, may cling [to me]; but let the intention of my mind, panting with love for you, attain to the work of justice and piety. And let my work be clean, and my prayer, as you command, in secret, so that I may not serve for the eye, as one pleasing to men. Allow me to know the admonitions of your laws and the most honourable deeds of the fathers, and grant me to fulfil them in deeds. Draw me back from every snare of sin, and keep me from the stain of all errors. Bind me always with the bars of your discipline, and hold me most firmly, so that I may not fall again. Draw me after you, and lead [me] wherever it pleases you, and by no means let me go back, turning my back again; may I be anxious in fear of you, perfect in love, constant in faith, in no way doubtful in hope; may I be fervent in love of my neighbour, not burn with the heat of hatred, nor waste away with the bruise of envy.

37. Always inspire holy work, that I may think of it; compel me, that I may do it; persuade me, that I may love it; confirm me, that I may hold it; guard me, that I may not lose it. Let pride, the mother and queen of the seven principal vices, not enter, nor rest in the dwelling of my heart, nor let her offspring cling to me, that is, gluttony, lust, fornication, avarice, envy, anger, sadness, vainglory. But give me, on the contrary, deep humility, by which the height of pride may be bowed; give measured abstinence, by which the excessive greed of the belly may be reined in. Give chastity, cleanness of heart, by which unclean lust may be lulled to sleep; give a will flowing freely to give alms, by which grasping avarice may be rejected. Give the love of perfect charity, by which the zeal of envy may be extinguished. Grant the patience of endurance, through which anger may be overcome and fail; bestow hope of eternal joy, by which the bitterness of sadness may be soothed; then make me so glory inwardly in my mind in you over good work, that the boasting of vainglory may not go out from me outwardly.

38. Grant me also to hold in all things justice, magnanimity, temperance; and make me prudent with simplicity, so that I may both lead the blessed life sincerely and prudently flee evil; and that the fraudulent and deceitful cunning of the devil may not deceive me under the appearance of good, so that I may be able both to discern [it] rationally and to foresee [it]; after this make me gentle and kindly, peaceable and meek, modest and bashful, reverent and fearful, fair, truthful without pretence, and reasonable without guile, in harmony with the good, constantly vigorous in vigils and fasts and prayer; grant also that I may keep my speech moderate in gentleness, and use from time to time a friendly silence, so that I may say what is fitting, and keep silent about what ought not to be spoken; and whatever of the fruits of virtues you deign to bestow, let humility as patron preserve it, with boasting put to death.

39. Grant that I may keep for you an unblemished faith, without any error of perverse religion, and be a worker worthy of the faith, so that I may not pollute right faith with wicked work; and that him whom I confess by believing well I may not deny by living badly; and him whom I follow with vigorous faith I may not offend by an act of negligence; make me, living in a holy resolve, follow justice, love mercy, love truth, reject falsehood, contemplate or speak nothing false, fear you unceasingly, venerate religion, keep peace with all without guile, call back the discordant to concord, offer charity without pretence, give scandal to no one, prefer myself to no one, but judge myself lower than the lowest, resist princes and powers in nothing, obey [them] in all things, show reverence and honour to elders, offer obedience and charity to equals, show the grace of fitting love to the young, bear the burdens or dangers of brothers with equanimity, venerate a friend as my own soul, love parent and neighbour as myself, and at the same time benefit all, not hinder, harm no one, oppose no one, slander no one, put a stumbling-block before no one, judge no one, disparage no one, condemn no one, be injurious to no one, carp at no one's life, pry into no one's right path, be anxious only about myself, by no means repay evil for evil, be in no way either mindful or an avenger of my injuries, but overcome all malice with goodness, prepare a blessing for one who curses, suffer adversities, not inflict them, love an enemy as a friend, bear the abuse and insults of angry men, not repay [them], quickly forget an injury, readily forgive one who has offended me, be always ready to grant pardon, not covet what belongs to others, nor take it away on any pretext, but mercifully give what is mine to those who have not, forgive the debtor his debt, restore what has been wrongfully seized, return the pledge to the borrower, and retain nothing belonging to another with me; then feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, take in the stranger, clothe the naked, visit the sick, seek out the prisoner, console the sad, suffer with the afflicted and mourning, provide necessities to one who has none, share food and clothing with the needy, embrace the native, cherish the member of the household, love the foreigner, ransom the captive, receive the newcomer, protect the ward and the orphan, support the widow, come to the aid of the oppressed, give help to the desolate, break the bonds of impiety, let the broken go free, and break every burden, as all the teachings of your precepts declare; to seek [them] ardently, read [them] diligently, consider [them] prudently, practise [them] promptly, fulfil [them] longingly.

40. Turn away, Lord, my eyes from vanity, and my steps from the paths of injustice. Let my ears not receive reproach against a neighbour; nor, abandoning the truth, itch to hear the tales of vanity or words of falsehood; nor let my tongue itch to disparage or curse a prince or a priest or any man after them. Let it not be scurrilous, nor vain-speaking, not abusive, not deceitful. May I not deceive my neighbour, calling his way good when perhaps it has shown itself wicked, but, moved by humble compassion, may I speak the truth privately, so that he may be turned from error, and if indeed he listens, his soul may be saved, and (as it is written) the multitude of my sins may be covered. May I be quick in hearing, moderate in answering. May I not be puffed up with knowledge, nor distended with the swelling of arrogance, but, abounding in good speech and work, may I always be humble, so that I may rise, not fall, be raised up, not overthrown, ascend, not descend. Let praises not corrupt me, nor reproaches disturb [me]; let flatteries not deceive [me], nor lies delude [me]; let prosperity not lift [me] up, nor adversity bow [me] down; let favourable opinion not exalt [me], nor unfavourable cast [me] down; let pleasantness not make me changeable, nor sadness make [me] unlike myself; but in all things let my life be even, and my countenance constant in one manner.

41. In health may I praise [you], in sickness give thanks, in correction not resist, under the scourge not murmur; may I not be exalted over good work, ascribe no good deed to myself, glory or trust in myself for nothing; but may you yourself be the glory, hope, strength, praise and all delight of my soul; may I believe you in my heart, confess you with praises, may my voice sound you, my tongue proclaim you continually; may I please you, not myself, and do your will, not mine, and may my whole mind meditate on you, delight in you, and my intention follow [you], so that, denying myself, I may follow you with my cross, ready to lose my soul for you, that through you I may find it; so that the furnace of penitence, all the thorns of vices being burnt up, may restore for you a new man out of useless oldness, and the last part of life may reform [the one] long most adorned with depravity, so that in this, errors renounced, the ancient enemy may in future recognise or find nothing of his own in me. Now therefore, Lord my God, with great exultation I glorify your holy name, you who persistently instructed my foolishness and softened my hardness through your scourges, until even unwillingly I heard your voices calling me for a long time, and, converted, followed the verse of the psalm now proclaiming to me: Bind fast with bit and bridle the jaws of those who do not draw near to you (Ps. 31:9). And I, Lord, have known and understood the sound of your cry, and reproving myself I have been converted, and have done penitence before you, as this day proves; therefore, to your praise and my consolation, let me sing to you the prophetic words: Chastise me, Lord, for I have been instructed, like an untamed young bullock.

42. For after you came to me, I did penitence; and after you showed me, I struck my thigh, I was confounded and blushed, because I bore the reproach of my youth, and I remembered my God, and said: I will confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ever (Ps. 117:1); for in your mercy my soul has come to life again and risen from the dead, because you have separated me from the sins of my youth, and from my youth you have rebuked me, and converted me, and I have done penitence before you. Therefore I have become a man of good hope, because you kept for me a time of conversion, in which, considering my sins, I was pierced with compunction and did penitence before you. Joyful now, I will henceforth render you countless thanks, now and always, imploring you with all my inmost being, commending myself to you with all devotion, because, that I might be found, you sought me; that I might return, you compelled me; that I might be struck, you looked upon [me]; that I might confess, you brought it about; that, recognising myself, I might lament, you granted it to me. Set my tears, Lord, in your sight, and let my prayer, [the prayer] of a publican and a sinner, come to you in heaven. Let the confession of my mouth be pleasing to you, and in place of the offerings of gifts, which I do not now offer, I submit to you as a sacrifice this weeping of my contrite heart; and receive this performance of penitence in place of acceptance, if that should be denied me, because the performance is enjoined by you, the acceptance is not required.

43. Be, Lord, my helper and protector unto salvation, and let your mercy follow me all the days of my life; and, placing me in joyful shades, refresh me, protecting me with the shadow of your wings. But when you bring on the day of my calling, behold, Lord, weeping I say, I shall enter, wretched, trembling and fearful, the way of most bitter death, most dark, unknown and without remedy, plunging into deep gloom. Be present, I pray, and come to my aid, and receive into your hands the spirit commended to you, freeing my soul from the mouth of the most savage dragon and from the hand of most dreadful hell, when you have received it; and take me out from the midst of the shadow of death; rather, lead me onto the shady path of light and the most bright region of the living. Place me, Lord, in the safest folds of your flocks, and number me, joined with your sheep, in the governance of the heavenly mansions, where your saints Abraham, Isaac and Jacob dwell, enjoying the pleasantness of light and refreshment, with the whole multitude of your saints; for you are the good shepherd, who lead out and lead back, seek what is lost and save what is found, cherish and heal what is sick; and you are the merciful Lord, who do not confound those who hope in you, do not abandon those who seek you, do not despise those who return to you, but receive [them] with exultation and praise, rejoicing more before your angels over one penitent and converted wanderer than over ninety-nine of the number of the blessed; to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one deity, glory, power, dominion and might for ever and ever. Amen.
